title: British Museum director Nicholas Cullinan: 'The Bayeux Tapestry, in a non-nationalistic way, is clearly part of our national identity'
subhead: With just seven days to go before the exhibition opens, the director of the British Museum, Nicholas Cullinan, reflects on the extraordinary journey involved in the loan and transfer of this monumental work from France to England.

subhead: On Tuesday, the Israeli prime minister insisted that the Hamas attacks on the morning of October 7, 2023, would have been contained if he had been woken earlier, but that his security officials intentionally decided not to do so.

title: Iran sentences photojournalist to 15 years in prison for sharing images of repression abroad
subhead: Accused of sending photographs to foreign media, Yalda Moaiery has just had her sentence upheld on appeal. In January, Le Monde published her images of the protests against the regime, in a rare testimonial.

title: The dangers of 'eating jet lag': Why eating at irregular hours is bad for your health
subhead: A large-scale French study suggests that men who eat meals at highly variable times between workdays and days off face an increased risk of cardiovascular disease.

title: 'With France seeking profound change, momentum lies only with candidates who promise to upend the status quo'
subhead: As speculation mounts over a possible second-round duel between far-right Marine Le Pen and radical left Jean-Luc Mélenchon in the 2027 French presidential election, no candidate from a party that has previously governed has managed to break through. This situation is having damaging effects, writes Le Monde columnist Françoise Fressoz.

title: 'Even our ancestors do not remember a flood of this scale:' Nepal villagers face apocalypse frozen in mud
subhead: Warned in time, many residents of Devighat managed to evacuate their homes just minutes before the mudslide killed over 900 people in Nepal and China. They have started to return to the village, where rescuers are still looking for survivors and the deceased in extremely perilous conditions.

title: 'No regulation exists:' Suez Canal becomes gateway for invasive species in the Mediterranean
subhead: 'Suez, a historic canal' (6/6). The opening of a passage between the Red Sea and the Mediterranean led to migrations of 'Lessepsian' species, named after the canal's developer, Ferdinand de Lesseps. Their proliferation, which destabilizes ecosystems, has increased due to overfishing, pollution, coastal building and climate change.
